items.body: Review by anomalocaris — This is an album I really love.Cressida's second album 'Asylum' differs quite a lot from their debut album. I will admit that I haven't listened to the entirety of their first album, but from the few songs I've heard, it sounds like some pretty decent rock. Asylum brings a new symphonic sound with some neat orchestrations. This is an album where every song (to me) feels basically perfect. You have 'Munich' and 'Let Them Come When They Will' which are your longer prog compositions, then there's 'Asylum', 'Goodbye Post Office Tower Goodbye', and 'Survivor' which are some shorter fun rock songs. 'Reprieved' is a short, jazzy, piano-led instrumental, and 'Lisa' is a great, shorter prog song with a lot of organs. I will say the song 'Summer Weekend Of A Lifetime' is quite boring to me and sort of feels like a filler song where the band had space for one more track and just threw together a little song. I love the orchestration in this album, particularly in the two longer, prog-ier tracks. 'Munich' also has this amazing epic sounding ending with a lot of brass instruments that I personally love. Those brass instruments can also be heard on the track 'Survivor'. This album is filled to the brim with organ and guitar solos, which I enjoy but may throw some listeners off.In short, if you're a fan of symphonic orchestrations and lots of guitar and organ solos, this is the perfect album for you.Oh yeah, did you know Mikael Akerfeldt of Opeth loves this band and album? (Stated in an interview with Progrock magazine in 2004)
items._genre: symphonic prog / progressive rock / classic rock
items._cn_summary: Cressida的第二张专辑《Asylum》相比首作融入了更丰富的交响化编曲，铜管乐器与管风琴、吉他独奏构成了听感核心。专辑包含两首较长的前卫摇滚作品《Munich》与《Let Them Come When They Will》，后者被评论者视为编排亮点；其余曲目多为短篇流行摇滚或器乐小品。整体属于七十年代初英国交响前卫摇滚的典型形态，编曲讲究但实验性有限，对熟悉坎特伯雷或早期Genesis一脉的听众可能仍有吸引力，但在更广阔的实验与前卫场景中位置较为边缘。

items.body: Carpenter Brut and HEALTH will reunite this autumn for “Conflict: Europe 2026”, the European continuation of their co-headlining partnership following the North American “Conflict: Leather Tour” earlier this year. The European run begins in Utrecht on November 3 and moves through the UK, Germany, Poland, Hungary and Italy, with VOWWS joining as special guests on the joint dates. The pairing works precisely because the two headliners arrive at heaviness from different directions. Carpenter Brut builds it through darksynth, metal dynamics, huge synthesizer hooks and cinematic excess, while HEALTH combine industrial electronics, distorted guitars, noise and vulnerable melodic songwriting. On the same bill, these approaches should create a particularly physical evening without simply repeating the same musical language twice. For Polish audiences, the tour brings two consecutive shows: November 16, 2026 – Kraków, Klub Studio – Carpenter Brut + HEALTH + VOWWS November 17, 2026 – Wrocław, Centrum Koncertowe A2 – Carpenter Brut + HEALTH + VOWWS The Polish concerts are promoted by Knock Out Productions. The European dates come after Carpenter Brut and HEALTH spent spring 2026 touring North America together, making this less of a one-off package and more of an ongoing collaboration between two acts whose audiences increasingly overlap across industrial, dark electronic, alternative and heavier scenes. ‘Conflict: Europe 2026’ tour dates Carpenter Brut, HEALTH and VOWWS play the following joint dates: November 3 – Utrecht, Netherlands – TivoliVredenburg November 4 – Bristol, UK – O2 Academy Bristol November 5 – Glasgow, UK – SWG3 Galvanizers November 6 – Wolverhampton, UK – Wulfrun Hall November 11 – Hamburg, Germany – Große Freiheit 36 November 13 – Leipzig, Germany – Täubchenthal November 16 – Kraków, Poland – Klub Studio November 17 – Wrocław, Poland – Centrum Koncertowe A2 November 19 – Budapest, Hungary – Barba Negra November 20 – Milan, Italy – Alcatraz About HEALTH HEALTH is an American industrial rock band formed in Los Angeles in 2005 by vocalist and guitarist Jake Duzsik and bassist John Famiglietti, who met while Duzsik was working at a Guitar Center store. Guitarist Jupiter Keyes and drummer BJ Miller joined soon after, giving the band its early lineup; Keyes left in 2015, and the group has continued as the trio of Duzsik, Famiglietti and Miller. HEALTH drew early attention with a remix of Crystal Castles’ “Crimewave” before releasing its self-titled debut album in 2007, followed by “Get Color” in 2009 and “Death Magic” via Loma Vista Recordings in 2015. “Vol. 4 :: Slaves of Fear” followed in 2019, and the band released the collaborative “Disco4” project across two volumes in 2020 and 2022. HEALTH issued “Rat Wars” in 2023, and its sixth studio album, “Conflict DLC”, followed via Loma Vista Recordings on December 11, 2025, preceded by the singles “Ordinary Loss”, “Vibe Cop”, “Thought Leader”, “You Died”, “Shred Envy” and “Antidote”. Los Angeles-based HEALTH have spent years developing a sound in which industrial electronics, noise, metal and pop melody are allowed to coexist without softening one another. One of the band’s most distinctive qualities remains the contrast between the enormous physical weight of the production and Duzsik’s comparatively restrained, vulnerable vocal delivery, which gives the music an emotional character very different from straightforward industrial aggression. The current touring cycle follows “Conflict DLC”, continuing the darker and heavier direction explored on “Rat Wars”. Live, that combination of mechanical rhythm, distortion and unexpectedly intimate vocals gives HEALTH a particularly strong physical and emotional presence, one that carries directly into the “Conflict: Europe 2026” dates. About Carpenter Brut Carpenter Brut is the project of French producer Franck Hueso, born in 1977 in Poitiers, who has cultivated anonymity as a deliberate artistic choice since starting the project in 2012 to mix horror-film scoring, metal, rock and electronic music. He first released three EPs, “EP I” (2012), “EP II” (2013) and “EP III” (2015), later compiled as the debut album “Trilogy” (2015). “Leather Teeth” followed in 2018, drawing on 1980s metal and glam rock and opening the fictional story of anti-hero Bret Halford. Hueso then scored the animated feature “Blood Machines” in 2020 before continuing the narrative with “Leather Terror” in 2022. He closed the trilogy with Leather Temple, released on February 27, 2026, which continues Bret Halford’s story into a cryogenic, cyberpunk-inflected future and closes out the “Leather” arc that began with “Leather Teeth”. Carpenter Brut approaches electronic heaviness from another angle than HEALTH. His music draws from synthwave, metal, horror cinema and 1980s pop culture, but over the years the project has moved far beyond simple retro aesthetics, developing into something much more aggressive, theatrical and designed for large live spaces. “Leather Temple” continues Carpenter Brut’s mixture of cinematic electronics, darksynth and metal while expanding the fictional world that has accompanied this chapter of the project, material that now anchors the “Conflict: Europe 2026” set. With VOWWS opening and two headliners whose methods of creating tension are so different, “Conflict: Europe 2026” looks like one of the more interesting dark electronic touring packages of the autumn, including the two Polish dates in Kraków and Wrocław.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. Further reading: The Young'uns - Tiny Notes (Review) Ben Nicholls - Duets

items.body: “Natural” moves at walking pace, a lovers rock groove kept soft under Clarence Bekker‘s blues-trained voice as it eases across the rocksteady sway. The new single from his Barcelona band is a plain love song from a singer with a long, loud history behind him. Bekker carries an unusual CV for a reggae singer: a UK chart entry in the 1990s as CB Milton, seven world tours, and a spell fronting the street-recorded Playing For Change project. Born in Suriname and raised in the Netherlands from the age of six, he cut his teeth in the Dutch group Swinging Soul Machine before that dance-pop run, then settled in Barcelona and, in 2016, built a band around local players. That band is a five-piece of Barcelona regulars: guitarist Francisco Guisado, known as Rubio, keyboardist Arecio Smith, bassist Charlie Cuevas and drummer Carlos López behind Bekker’s vocals. They hold a weekly Thursday residency at the jazz club Jamboree and have carried the same lineup as far as Australia and Brazil. The song came together between Barcelona and the road, Bekker recording while Irish lyricist Michael Leahy sent words over from wherever he was travelling, a habit going back to their fax-machine days writing CB Milton hits together in the 90s. Everyone in the band had a hand in it, and it holds to the idea in its title: an unhurried love song, played the easy way. It is the first single from an album due later this year. Listen to “Natural” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Clarence Bekker Band – Natural appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 这是Clarence Bekker乐队发布的一首单曲，节奏舒缓，呈现lovers rock风格。乐队主唱Bekker有着横跨舞曲与街头录音项目的丰富履历，常驻巴塞罗那，五位固定成员每周在Jamboree爵士俱乐部演出。这首歌的创作跨越巴塞罗那与旅途，由爱尔兰词作者远程协作完成。整首歌气质从容、风格朴素，延续了乐队多年来的稳定编排路线。作为一首传统结构的情歌，它在编曲上保持了轻松易懂的取向，与实验性、前卫性或电子融合的方向距离较远，更偏向于成熟的现场演绎型作品。专辑预计今年晚些时候发行，这首单曲仅是其前奏。

多様性のあるレパートリーの構築を目指して、日本と英国を拠点に活動。東京藝術大学音楽学部附属音楽高等学校を経て同大学音楽学部器楽科卒業、同声会賞を受賞。英国王立音楽院修... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 夏のロンドンはシーズン・オフで、演奏会はBBCプロムスに集中する。本稿ではプロムス全体のプログラムを見渡しつつ、閑散期の隠れた名演をレポートしたい。 今年のプロムスではアメリカ合衆国建国250年を記念して、アメリカ系の作品が例年より多く登場する。しかしガーシュウィンやコープランド、バーンスタインら一部の作曲家に偏っていることは否定できまい。なお山田和樹は、バーミンガム市交響楽団とジョン・アダムズの合唱作品《ハルモニウム》に臨む。 プロムスらしく随所に散りばめられた現代作品のなかには、ベッツィ・ジョラス（『音楽の友』2026年8月号でレポート）やジェシー・モンゴメリー、ジョーン・タワーなどアメリカ系作曲家の作品も見受けられる。しかし作曲家のジェンダー比率の均衡を図った結果、存命の作曲家では女性表象のアーティストが多い。権力勾配の不均衡を是正するクオータ制のやりかたでいえば、マイノリティ属性の人数をいったん増やすのは正解だが、西洋クラシック音楽の場合には「死んでいる作曲家」の扱いも工夫できるはずだ。平たくいえば、もっと「歴史上の女性」と「いまを生きる男性」を入れないと不都合をこうむる世代ができてしまう。 本来プロムスが始まって間もない20世紀前半は、エセル・スマイスの歌劇《The Wreckers》やドロシー・ハウエルの交響詩《Lamia》が人気を博すなど、女性作曲家は「そこに普通にいた」。歴史を踏まえて見ると2026年のラインナップは生ぬるい。 むしろ今年頻出するのはR・シュトラウスで、《ツァラトゥストラはかく語りき》、《死と変容》、《アルプス交響曲》や「歌劇《ナクソス島のアリアドネ》」に「《ばらの騎士》組曲」、そして《英雄の生涯》、《4つの最後の歌》と充実。またベルリオーズが「序曲《ローマの謝肉祭》」、《幻想交響曲》、「レクイエム」、《ファウストの劫罰》と並ぶのは珍しい。 プロムスといえば、大編成の金管や打楽器を浴びるように聴くのが醍醐味で、先の2巨頭に加え、エルガーやヴォーン・ウィリアムズ、ウォルトンの交響曲、そして初日に奏でられたフィンジ《聖チェチーリアのために》といった英国の大規模作品は、この音楽祭ならではの聴き応えがあろう。 また今年はマーラーも交響曲が5曲とたっぷり聴けるが、ブルックナー作品がゼロで寂しい。なおプロムスはBBCのサイトでラジオ中継を配信しており、日本からも無料で再生可能だ。 BBCプロムスのメイン会場、ロイヤル・アルバート・ホール ©原田真帆 ロンドンを拠点とする楽団の首席奏者たちが室内楽を奏でる「チェンバー・プリンシパルズ・オブ・ロンドン」 そんなプロムス開幕前夜。ウォータールー駅の高架のふもとにある 1901 Arts Club にて、チェンバー・プリンシパルズ・オブ・ロンドンの演奏会を聴いた。この団体はロンドンを拠点とする楽団の首席奏者によって構成されており、メンバーたちがふだん奏でる大規模な管弦楽曲とは打って変わって、より親密な室内楽の公演を実施している。 この夜はロイヤル・オペラ・ハウス管弦楽団のコンサートマスターであるセルゲイ・レヴィティンと第2ヴァイオリン首席のヤン・シュモルクが、2台ヴァイオリンのために書かれた楽曲で鮮やかに魅せた。 まずは定番のルクレール「ソナタ」から「第4番」で開始。日ごろバレエ・ダンサーを支えているだけあって、舞踏家ルクレールの音を絶妙に引き出していく。かと思えば、シュポア「デュオ・コンチェルタンテ第2番」では、まるで管弦楽を聴いているような錯覚に陥る。 そしてシュニトケ《Moz-Art》ではコントさながらの演技力を見せる。演奏の前に奏者が台詞を言っていたのだが、楽器を鳴らしてもそれが言葉の続きのようで、ふだんから共に演奏しているからこその音のせめぎ合いは演劇のごとし。 終曲のハルヴォルセン《ノルウェー民謡による演奏会奇想曲》は、ふたりが代わるがわる協奏曲の独奏と伴奏を務めているかのようだ。通常は歌劇場のピットのなかで繰り広げられる職人技に、45人弱の小規模会場で間近に触れる贅沢な時間だった（7月16日）。
items._cn_summary: 本文报道2026年BBC逍遥音乐节开幕盛况，重点介绍美国建国250周年纪念曲目编排，包括格什温、科普兰、伯恩斯坦等美国作曲家作品，以及贝茨·乔拉斯、杰西·蒙哥马利等当代美国作曲家新作。文章同时回顾了R·施特劳斯、柏辽兹的大型管弦乐作品在节目中的高频出现，并指出马勒与布鲁克纳的比重差异。此外还报道了开幕前夜在1901 Arts Club举行的伦敦首席室内乐演奏会，罗亚尔歌剧院管弦乐团首席小提琴家莱维京与扬·施莫尔克演奏了勒克莱尔、施波尔、施尼特凯与哈尔沃森的双小提琴作品，以亲民形式展现职业演奏家的精湛技艺。

items.body: This is Deutsche Grammophon’s fourth album of Joe Hisaishi’s music. One recording (played by the Royal Philharmonic) is A Symphonic Celebration of selected film scores, but the others, including this latest release, focus on concert music. Metaphysica Amazon Presto Apple The album opens with Hisaishi’s Symphony No. 3 “Metaphysica”. The work was premiered by the New Japan Philharmonic in 2021 and was inspired by the music of Gustav Mahler: Hisaishi says it uses the same orchestration as Mahler’s first symphony, and it was programmed with that work at the premiere. The composer writes that the subtitle “Metaphysica” (Latin for “metaphysics”) refers to a philosophy “concerning the understanding of existence and knowledge.” The music “emphasizes logic that transcends sensation and experience,” and, in his words, “I aimed to create music composed solely of the movement of sound.” In three movements, the first (titled “existence”) is built around a rhythm “consisting of three sixteenth notes” that is heard in each movement, with “melodic movements that transform upon this foundation.” The second (“where are we going?”) grows from a single 26-measure phrase subjected to all manner of variations. The finale (“substance”) is built on a hexatonic scale which, in the composer’s words, is “placed on both the time and spatial axis.” I am hesitant to critique a composer’s style, as listeners’ tastes differ and my reaction may not be shared by others. So let me state straight away that Hisaishi is a minimalist, a school of composition I have struggled to understand and appreciate for most of my life. His orchestration is expert and was the most enjoyable aspect of my listening. One can find online descriptions of his memorable melodies, but I did not find that to be the case here. Nor does the symphony use expected Classical-Romantic structures: in the outer movements I listened for elements of sonata form, in which multiple themes are presented, developed, and recapitulated. Instead, Hisaishi builds his music by presenting a melodic motive and subjecting it to coloristic variation. That orchestration held my interest for a long stretch; Hisaishi’s music is atmospheric and cinematic. But the three-note rhythm meant to bind the three movements together was not evident to me, even after repeated listening, nor was the melodic writing memorable. The ostinatos and continuing variations felt overused, and by the third movement I struggled to stay focused on the music. Excepting continuous variation, I am not sure how Hisaishi’s music connects to Mahler’s symphonic world, though his notes on the symphony suggest that was his intent. Not a revelatory discovery for me, though others may react differently. Joe Hisaishi. Photo © Nick Rutter. The Harp Concerto was a joint commission by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Bordeaux National Opera, the Philharmonie de Paris, and the Singapore Symphony Orchestra, written for Emmanuel Ceysson, the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s principal harpist. Ceysson collaborated with the composer, both in Los Angeles and Japan, during its composition. Deutsche Grammophon’s notes state that the work “reimagines the expressive possibilities of the harp,” replacing “conventional notions of delicacy with driving rhythms, bold gestures, and striking emotional intensity.” The concerto proved a more engaging listening experience. I sensed less reliance on ostinato writing — or perhaps the more substantial melodic writing and Western harmonic progressions made it seem so. The writing is more memorable; even after the first listening, parts of the work remained in my head. And the music does succeed in reimagining the instrument’s expressive possibilities, especially in the outer movements, which feature dazzling playing from Ceysson. The highlight for me, though, was the poignant second movement, which ends with a substantial coda demonstrating both the technique and musicianship of the soloist. Disappointingly, the digital release does not include any liner notes. The Royal Philharmonic play splendidly, though they sound more engaged by the concerto than the symphony. The recording is spacious and clear. One assumes that with the composer conducting, the music goes exactly as he intends. If you enjoyed this album, also hear Joe Hisaishi in Vienna (Symphony No. 2, Viola Saga) | Joe Hisaishi Conducts (Hisaishi & Reich) | A Symphonic Celebration (Studio Ghibli) | de Maistre: Harp Concertos (Glière, Mosolov) The form can be filled in the actual website url. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了久石让的《第三交响曲》与竖琴协奏曲。《第三交响曲》受马勒第一交响曲配器启发，三个乐章分别探讨存在、走向与本体，运用持续变化手法而非传统奏鸣曲式构建音乐。乐评指出其管弦乐配器精湛、氛围具有电影感，但作者作为长期对极简主义持保留态度的听众，认为三连音节奏在三个乐章间的贯穿不够明显，旋律记忆点不足，固定音型与变奏在第三乐章显得冗长。与马勒的联系也较为牵强。竖琴协奏曲部分内容未在截取的乐评中展开。整体而言，这是一张面向主流古典听众的当代作品，与实验性、前卫性音乐路线存在明显距离。

items.body:
Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.
Berceuse
Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

INTERNATIONAL（海外）
NEWS
豪州７都市を巡回「Japan Jazz Nights」
「日豪友好協力基本条約」署名50周年記念
2026年8月11日
編集部

「日豪友好協力基本条約」署名50周年を記念し2026年10月にオーストラリア７都市（アデレード、キャンベラ、シドニー、ホバート、パース、ブリスベン、メルボルン）を巡るジャズ巡回公演「Japan Jazz Nights」が予定されている。

この公演には、国際的にも注目を集める４組のアーティスト（BIGYUKI、STEREO CHAMP、Tenors In Chaos、梅井美咲）が出演、公演では一部、現地のアーティストとのコラボレーションも予定されており、音楽を通じて両国の相互理解を深め、日豪間の文化交流のさらなる発展を目指しているという。国際交流基金の交流事業の一環として実施される

Big Yuki
Stereo Champ
Tenors in Chaos
梅井美咲

items.body: The NWOSM (new wave of satirical metalcore) saw its resurgence with one band and one band only: Electric Callboy. I'm of the generation where hyper-energetic, Pixy Stix-snorting acts are either harshly condemned or praised to oblivion, and after I caught whiff of Electric Callboy's rejection to be the German entrant for the 2002 Eurovision Song Contest with the song "Pump It," I fell into a strict limbo. On one hand, I appreciated how the band took absolutely nothing seriously and still drew in tens of millions of views, but I deemed myself unready to earnestly listen to a full-length album of their uber-loud, electronic material. At the time, my adrenaline levels couldn't possibly handle the onslaught of cheesy choruses, the electronicore production, and the relentless attitude of the sextet. Fortunately, I've grown as a listener and as a reviewer, and Electric Callboy has given me a prospect to listen to fourteen whole tracks on their seventh LP, Tanzneid.Well, less than fifteen percent are truly brand-new. The final four pieces are remixes of both past and current cuts, with "Heartclub" and "The Savior" as the sole fresh songs. Singles for Tanzneid trace all the way to 2024–"Ratatata," featuring Babymetal, was released on the Tokyo-based, kawaii collective's latest record, already over a year old. The other singles create a timeline of anticipation, which is understandable given the context of modern marketing tactics, but it dilutes the ultimate impact of a new album releasing new music. In essence, Tanzneid isn't all that new.That doesn't mean the album isn't enjoyable, however. Its forefront focuses on hosting gimmicks, like Eurodance-infused breakdowns on the title-track, collaborations with established artists like The Offspring on "Let The Good Times Roll", pairings of wildly different styles, like rap metal/elevator music in "Elevator Operator", and tongue-in-cheek pop culture parodies, with Backstreet Boys-turned-deathcore number "The Way You Are" ironically being one of the harshest songs in terms of vocals, all situated closely together running order. Each piece achieves these merits within a digestible, radio-ready runtime and never comes off too farcical. Electric Callboy thrive in satire, meaning that weaker tracks—the ones that have no direct sonic gimmick—are unmemorable. These are shoved to the latter half of the album. The momentum doesn't hold for long though, sadly. At the halfway point, they begin instead to rely heavily on electronic metalcore that's comparably domestic compared to Callboy's rabidness. Even a duet with Frank Zummo of Sum 41 fame can't propel "Still Waiting" from the stretch of forgettability. When Electric Callboy abstain from silliness is when they start to chameleon themselves with the incoming waves of electronicore. "Heartclub," amongst other straightforward compositions, is unexpectedly brutal without any outside influence to contort its atmosphere, sitting in torpor amongst Scene-esque territories that the band supposedly ditched after their name switch. Tanzneid further overstays its welcome with some nine minutes of extra remixws, showing that they're still holding onto their past.I wouldn't mind hearing ten back-to-back gimmicks if it meant that Electric Callboy had freedom to poke fun at and experiment with as many styles as they please. It feels unorthodox to suggest that a band lean deeper into trivial, parodic themes, but for an entity like Electric Callboy who are already immersed in frantic craziness, I wanted to hear some truly hilarious music, with enough metal to mosh to. I chuckled, but guffaws were few across the multicolored brain of Tanzneid. This full album stream is like a compilation of the music videos. A mini-movie, of sorts.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以讽刺金属核为核心框架，混杂大量欧陆舞曲、说唱金属与流行文化戏仿元素，如后街男孩风格的死亡金属拼贴、与The Offspring和Sum 41成员的跨界合作。制作上偏向电台友好的短时长结构，电子核音色占主导，偶有合成器化的breakdown。乐评指出专辑后半段失去了前期恶搞带来的新鲜感，回归直白的电子金属核编排，使得缺乏明确噱头的曲目陷入平庸。整体定位是面向大众市场的趣味性重型音乐，新歌比例不足两成，包含四首旧作混音。商业发行策略痕迹明显，单曲早在2024年便陆续释出，削弱了新专辑的完整叙事感。

items._cn_summary: 英国新浪漫浪潮的代表乐队Haircut 100在解散44年后推出回归专辑《Boxing The Compass》。主创尼克·海沃德的嗓音依然保持着青春时期的清亮质感，乐队成员的演奏呈现出多年沉淀后的紧凑与成熟，旋律编排轻快爽朗。整体呈现出老牌乐队复活后常见的怀旧延续风格，依托当年的经典配方重新演绎，但在声音探索和实验性上鲜有突破。乐队此前凭借首张专辑《Pelican West》在82年代走红，如今的续作更像是向早年风格的一次温情致敬，而非音乐方向上的拓展尝试。对于熟悉该乐队历史的老听众而言，这张作品具备一定的情感价值，但从音乐创新的维度审视，并未带来超出预期的内容。

items.body: 山下達郎のライブアルバム『JOY 2 / TATSURO YAMASHITA LIVE』が2026年10月14日（水）にリリースされることが決定した。 ここ数年、ファンの間で渇望され、山下達郎本人の口からも制作状況が都度語られてきたライブアルバム『JOY 2 / TATSURO YAMASHITA LIVE』が遂に完成した。山下達郎のライブ盤は1978年に発売された『IT’S A POPPIN’ TIME』、1989年に発売された『JOY』の2作品に続き、通算3作目。前作『JOY』からはなんと37年ぶり、まさにファン待望のリリースとなる。 2008年から2025年までの18年間で実施した13本の全国ツアー、600を超える公演から山下達郎本人がベストオブベストテイクを厳選した、3枚組全38トラックで構成される本作。ディスク1には“SPARKLE”“DONUT SONG”“僕らの夏の夢”“土曜日の恋人”“風の回廊（コリドー）”“さよなら夏の日”“THE THEME FROM BIG WAVE”などライブには欠かせない定番曲に加え、初期の名作である“CIRCUS TOWN”や近年のヒットナンバー“SYNC OF SUMMER”まで16トラックが収められる。 ディスク2には“WINDY LADY”や“PAPER DOLL”“BOMBER”を挟んだ“SILENT SCREAMER”のほか、“恋のブギ・ウギ・トレイン”など山下達郎のライブの真骨頂とも言える10トラックを収録。 ディスク3には“人力飛行機”“ミライのテーマ”などの比較的新しめのナンバーに加え、“蒼氓（そうぼう）”“ずっと一緒さ”などの染み入るナンバー、さらには“高気圧ガール”“アトムの子”“RIDE ON TIME”などのタツロークラシックから最新曲“MOVE ON”まで幅広い選曲で12トラックが収められる。 また、初回盤にのみ付属するディスク4には、既発シングルのボーナストラックだったライブ音源6トラックが新たなミックスを施して収録されるほか、ツアーではおなじみの“LET’S DANCE BABY”のメドレー箇所だけをエディットした2010年、2012年、2014年のバージョンの3トラックも用意。合計9トラックというファン垂涎のボーナスディスクとなっている。 ソロデビュー50周年という節目の年に遂に登場するライブアルバム『JOY 2』。発売を楽しみに待とう。

items.excerpt: 2026.08.11 毎週火曜日更新！ Q. 長い間、バッハの自筆譜だと思われていた《無伴奏チェロ組曲》の楽譜。実際に書いたのは誰でしょう？ バッハの代表作《無伴奏チェロ組曲》。実は長い間、ある楽譜が「バッハ本人の自筆譜」だと考えられていました。 では、その楽譜を書いたのは？ A. 妻アンナ・マグダレーナ B. 息子カール・フィリップ・エマヌエル C. 一番弟子ヨハン・ケルナー こたえ A. 妻アンナ・マグダレーナ 実はその楽譜は、妻アンナ・マグダレーナが清書した写譜でした。 彼女の筆跡はあまりにも夫によく似ていたため、長い間「バッハ本人の自筆譜」と考えられていたほど。 夫婦で楽譜を書き、音楽を作り上げていた……そんな仲の良さが伝わってくるエピソードです。 解説の続きはこちら！ バッハとアンナ・マグダレーナ～筆跡から見える音楽史上最高の仲良し夫婦

items.body: 2026.08.11 NTT西日本のオープンイノベーション施設「QUINTBRIDGE」交流イベント 吹奏楽業界で近年、大きな課題とされている「部活動の地域展開」は、文科省の予算が圧倒的に不足していると言われるなか、現場の閉塞感が高まっている。吹奏楽部をどのように地域展開させるのか、そのアイデアを異なる業界の人たちと交流することで考えようというイベントが5月行われた。 和田響子 編集部 埼玉県出身。DTPや自転車など専門誌の編集部を経て、音楽之友社に入社。2015〜2022年3月に編集部のWeb担当として、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」やオンラインシ... 詳しく見る 部活動は2026年度からの6年間で「改革実行」へ 大阪市の京橋駅近くにあるオープンイノベーション施設「QUINTBRIDGE（クイントブリッジ）」。NTT西日本の本社ビルの敷地内に2022年に創設され、世の中をもっとよくしたいと考える人々が集い共創する場として、ワークショップやモノづくり、入居する会員の事業が行われている。 この「新たな出会いフロア」と呼ばれる1階で、5月15日、「部活動（吹奏楽）の地域展開を考える ― 地域と企業がともに描く、これからの“文化の支え方” 」と題するイベントが開催された。 部活動の地域展開とは 文科省が主導する部活動改革の一環。教員不足の原因のひとつとされる教員の長時間労働を是正するための「教員の働き方改革」に端を発し、「部活動のガイドライン」で活動時間などの制限について目安が提示されたうえ、公立中学校の部活動を教員に負担させないために、運営主体を地域（民間）に「展開」しようと各自治体が中心となって進められている。 すでに「改革推進期間」の3年間を終えて、2026年度から6年間の「改革実行期間」に入った。現状、休日については、過疎地域を中心に多くの地域で実施されはじめているが、平日に関してはさらに課題山積で、ごく一部の地域での実施に留まっている。 減少が危惧されている吹奏楽部の課題 吹奏楽部は、もっとも地域展開が難しい部活動とされている。 なぜなら、楽器や楽譜といった「備品」や、音出しが可能な「練習場所」は、学校部活動の練習環境だからこそ毎日のように使用できるものだからだ。学校の音楽室は、体育館のように独立した建物でない場合がほとんどなので、地域クラブの運営者が利用する場合は、セキュリティの問題を解決しなければならない。 また、吹奏楽にはおもに12種類の楽器があって、本来それらの指導ができる「専門人材」も必要だが、これまでは教員の献身的な努力を中心に、先輩が後輩を教える伝統的なスタイル、場合によっては外部講師を招くということで、何とか成り立たせてきた。 そのほか、コンクールや演奏会での「楽器運搬」費などもあり、活動費は運動部よりも高額になりがちだ。これまでは自治体からの補助金などで工面できていた部分があるが、地域展開して国や自治体の予算が不足している現状のままであれば、習い事の月謝と変わらない金額を受益者（保護者）が負担することになるだろう。そうすると、子どもが入部できるかどうかは親の判断にも左右されて、吹奏楽ができる子どもが限られてしまう。 こうした課題が横たわる吹奏楽部の地域展開だが、だからと言って、このままでよいという話にはならないだろう。急激な少子化により、1つの学校では合奏できる人数に満たない地域も増えているうえ、教員不足を解消するには働き改革が急務だからだ。 小中学校の団体数や部員数の減少を数字で説明 未来のクラブ活動の姿を民間の事業が提案！ さて、こうした課題に対して、QUINTBRIDGEのイベントでは民間企業、行政、学校の立場から、さまざまな解決案が提示された。筆者は後日に記録動画を拝見したのだが、どの登壇者もプレゼンテーションの熱量が高くて面白く、ポジティブに未来を捉えた発表だったことは、まず言っておきたい。 民間からは4人が登壇し、画期的なテクノロジーやサービスが紹介された。 まずは「離れていてもtonari（隣り）で過ごそう」というキャッチコピーで他のシステムと一線を画す遠隔コミュニケーションシステム「tonari」。床から天井までを映す大型スクリーン、タイムラグを感じることない通信技術、そしてカメラを意識せずに目線を合わせて等身大の相手と話ができるスクリーン内蔵型カメラを備える。吹奏楽の現場であれば、リモートでの指導や合奏が自然に行えるのではないかと期待が膨らんだ。導入コストの高さが課題だが、普及するのであれば、生徒の移動や楽器運搬の問題が解決でき、地域格差の是正につながるだろう。 NTT西日本グループからは、全国20以上の自治体と連携して社会実装を進めている自動運転EVバスが紹介された。山口県周南市では、2024年度から実証実験がはじまり、すでにNavya Mobility製の自動運転EVバスが街を走っていて、満車のことも多いという。バスやタクシーのドライバーの高齢化や不足を改善するだけでなく、生徒の移動手段として利用できる日も近いかもしれない。 そのほか、服部管楽器が学校にある「休眠楽器」を修理して格安にレンタルすることを検討していること、また、就活支援と企業の人事コンサルティングを行うHUB@LIFEが、「仕事ができる人に吹奏楽経験者が多い」と企業にアピールし、スポンサーになってもらいつつ学生とつなぐ場としてコンサートを開催していることを紹介した。 この日の登壇者を紹介するスライド 地域クラブを大人のバンドの下部組織に 学校や地域の現場からは、すでに動き出している事例として、まず西宮市立中学校の教員・吹奏楽部顧問が、外部に受け皿となる組織をつくった例が紹介された。 大人の吹奏楽団の下部組織に中学生対象のジュニアバンドをいくつかの地域につくり、当初から指導者を用意して演奏会など本番の予定も組み、活動をパッケージにして提示。これにより、生徒や保護者の活動への不安が軽減できたとのこと。 「どこかのジュニアバンドが縮小しても、バンドを統合したり、小学5年生から社会人まで入れる大人のバンドが受け皿になって、子どもたちの活動は守られる」と語った。前述したような吹奏楽ならではの課題はあるものの、指導者など大人たちのつながりによって支えられる好例となるかもしれない。 学校を「まち」に ！ 地域住民にも活動の場をつくる北海道安平町 自治体からは、北海道安平町教育委員会の教育長である井内聖氏がオンラインで登壇。安平町は人口は7000人ほど、小学校1校、中学校1校のほか、小中一貫の義務教育学校が1校あるが、子どもも大人も減り、スポーツ・文化に取り組む機会も減っている。この機会を支援するため、学校内に「まち」をつくった経緯や現状を語った。 安平町立中学校の部活動は令和7年度までですべて廃止にして、地域クラブの練習場所、時間、送迎、活動費については教育委員会が主導して調整を図った。地域おこし協力隊と総合型スポーツクラブが、スポーツ・文化活動の運営をサポートし、希望する指導者や教職員の兼職兼業によって指導者を確保。中学生だけでは成り立たないので、小学生から大人まで多世代のために環境構築を進めた。 このプロセスで、令和5年4月に義務教育学校として新設される予定だった安平町立早来学園をどのようにつくり、地域に開放するかが議論された。 この学校の空間デザインを担当したのが、デジタルアートのクリエイティブで知られるチームラボだ。顔認証によるセキュリティを導入するなど、テクノロジーを活用して、大中2つの体育館や図書館、家庭科室のほか、音楽室、美術室、技術室といった学校施設を、公民館のように地域とシェアし、ほぼ毎日9時から21時まで地域の人が簡単に利用できるようにした。 顔認証システムを導入し、地域住民が自由に出入りできる安平町立早来学園の図書館の様子が映し出された たとえば、平日の日中に学校内で、シニアの健康教室、子育て支援、料理教室などが開かれ、0歳から90歳が集うなか、休み時間には学校の子どもたちも本を借りに来る。昼休みに図書館で弦楽四重奏のコンサートを開き、シニアやお母さんと赤ちゃんといった地域住民に加え、先生、生徒が自由に集まり、食いつくように演奏を聴く――そんな自然に交流が生まれる光景も映像で紹介され、孤立や分断のない「まち」の姿の一つだと感銘を受けた。 吹奏楽部は今年度から地域クラブになり、この学校内で活動している。中心となる外部講師だけでなく、各楽器の講師も協力して指導にあたり、オンラインレッスンも活用している。今年は小学生1名を含む15名が所属。遠くから通う子どももいるため、平日16〜17時は自主練習、17〜19時で合奏などの全体練習を行い、保護者の理解も得ながら順調に活動しているそうだ。 ここに至るまでには、現場との意見の相違もあったそうだが、井内氏は「10年後のスポーツ・文化環境は、どうなっているだろうか」と関係者に問いかけ、「残すために」必要な形を模索していった。井内氏は、予測できない未来をどう予測するのか、「無理・難しい」の先にあるものは何か、それが吹奏楽がなくなるという未来であれば、私たちはそれを受け入れるのか――そう訴え、理解を得ようと努めたそうだ。 現状を変えることはエネルギーがいるが、まわりの変化が激しいなかで、何も行動しないことは逆にリスクになり得る。多くの地域住民が学校になごやかに集い、中学生だけでない多世代で多様なクラブ活動が行われている安平町の映像からは、この判断によって町全体の幸福度も高まったのではと感じられた。 オンラインで登壇した、北海道安平町教育委員会の井内聖教育長 財源を確保しながら、民間の力で魅力ある地域展開を 昭和の時代から続いてきた日本の部活動文化は、学校教育の一環としてその意義を評価されてきた。文科省の「部活動改革及び地域クラブ活動の推進等に関する総合的なガイドライン」（2025年12月）にもあるように、地域クラブになったとしても、その教育的意義は守っていくことが望まれている。 ただ、日本のスポーツ・文化や教育への投資が諸外国と比べても少なく、地域展開についても予算が不足している状況のなか、この改革の負担を現場の運営者や指導者、保護者に強いれば、スポーツ・文化は衰退してしまう（すでに小中学生の吹奏楽団体・人口は、明らかに減少している）。 公教育の一環として子どもの「機会均等」を守るためには、今回QUINTBRIDGEで発表されたような民間のアイデアを活用できるように、まず行政がしっかりと財源を確保しなくてはならないだろう。それが地域全体も活性化するような「魅力ある地域展開」に導くことになるのではと考えさせられる機会だった。 おカネがかかる芸術教育〜国際比較から考える日本の課題と活路

items._cn_summary: 本文并非音乐评论，而是关于日本吹奏乐（管乐合奏）部活动从学校向地域社会转型的行业报道。文章以2026年5月在NTT西日本创新设施QUINTBRIDGE举办的研讨会为切入点，讨论了文部科学省推动的部活动改革背景下，吹奏乐社团面临乐器设备、练习场所、专业指导人才和活动经费等多重挑战。文中介绍了民间企业提出的远程合奏系统、自动驾驶EV巴士用于学生移动、休眠乐器租赁再利用等解决方案，以及西宫市和北海道安平町将中学生乐队纳入成人乐团旗下或在校内构建社区文化空间的实际案例。文章内容与用户的实验、前卫、爵士、电子等音乐偏好完全无关，属于教育政策与社区文化运营领域的新闻性报道。

items.album: 全国の音高生が一堂に！21校、116名が参加した真夏の合同オーケストラ

items.excerpt: 2026.08.10 全国の音楽高校の学生が集まり、一つの音楽をつくり上げる「全国音楽高等学校合同オーケストラ演奏会」が、7月25日に東京の国立オリンピック記念青少年総合センターで開催。全国音楽高等学校協議会に加盟する62の高等学校のなかから、21校、116名が参加した。 道下京子 音楽評論家 2019年夏、息子が10歳を過ぎたのを機に海外へ行くのを再開。 1969年東京都大田区に生まれ、自然豊かな広島県の世羅高原で育つ。子どもの頃、ひよこ（のちにニワトリ）... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 初めての仲間と音を響かせる 全国から集ったメンバーは、それぞれの学校から推薦を受けた生徒。練習から本番までともに過ごし、一つのプログラムを創り上げていく。 指揮は現田茂夫。そして、コンサートマスターは、3曲それぞれ演奏順に東京藝術大学音楽学部附属音楽高等学校の本村菜々花、国立音楽大学附属高等学校の伊藤諒柊
items.body: 2026.08.10 全国の音楽高校の学生が集まり、一つの音楽をつくり上げる「全国音楽高等学校合同オーケストラ演奏会」が、7月25日に東京の国立オリンピック記念青少年総合センターで開催。全国音楽高等学校協議会に加盟する62の高等学校のなかから、21校、116名が参加した。 道下京子 音楽評論家 2019年夏、息子が10歳を過ぎたのを機に海外へ行くのを再開。 1969年東京都大田区に生まれ、自然豊かな広島県の世羅高原で育つ。子どもの頃、ひよこ（のちにニワトリ）... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 初めての仲間と音を響かせる 全国から集ったメンバーは、それぞれの学校から推薦を受けた生徒。練習から本番までともに過ごし、一つのプログラムを創り上げていく。 指揮は現田茂夫。そして、コンサートマスターは、3曲それぞれ演奏順に東京藝術大学音楽学部附属音楽高等学校の本村菜々花、国立音楽大学附属高等学校の伊藤諒柊、桐朋女子高等学校音楽科（男女共学）の田遠麗奈が務めた。 演奏会は、チャイコフスキー「幻想序曲《ロミオとジュリエット》」で始まった。低弦楽器がたっぷりと音を鳴り響かせ、ヴァイオリンなどがメロディをロマンティックに歌い上げる。続くモーツァルト《ディヴェルティメント》では、楽器ごとの親密な対話を生み出していた。休憩をはさんで、ベートーヴェン「交響曲第8番」。テーマやモティーフを丁寧に表わし、豊かな響きを作り出す。また、ハーモニーの変化に耳を傾け、音色を多彩に表現していく姿が心に残る。そして、音楽を次第に高揚させ、圧倒的なクライマックスを形成していた。 音楽高校は近年、少子化にともなって廃止されたり、オーケストラの授業が困難になっていたりするという。オーケストラ作品への取り組みや、その成果をコンサートホールで聴衆に披露した経験は、今後の彼らの活動に結びついていくに違いない。 若さあふれる熱演に、客席からは盛大な拍手がおくられた 公演データ 全国音楽高等学校合同オーケストラ演奏会 〈日程・会場〉7月25日・国立オリンピック記念青少年総合センター 大ホール 〈出演〉現田茂夫（指揮）、全国音楽高等学校協議会加盟校生徒 〈曲目〉チャイコフスキー「幻想序曲《ロミオとジュリエット》」、モーツァルト《ディヴェルティメント》、ベートーヴェン「交響曲第7番」
items._cn_summary: 本文报道了2026年7月25日在东京国立奥林匹克纪念青少年综合中心举行的全国音乐高中合同管弦乐演奏会，来自全国21所音乐高中的116名学生参与演出，指挥为现田茂夫。曲目包括柴可夫斯基《罗密欧与朱丽叶幻想序曲》、莫扎特《嬉游曲》以及贝多芬《第八交响曲》。文章以新闻报道形式记录了这场学生联合演出活动，对各曲目的演奏进行了简要描述，并指出在少子化背景下音乐高中管弦乐课程面临困境，此类演出对学生未来的音乐道路具有积极意义。内容为活动新闻稿而非原创乐评，信息量有限。

items.album: Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat
items.excerpt: Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot. Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. items.body: Sorrow Stories, the project of UK artist Tina Forlorn, has released “So Sick”, her second collaboration with Christopher Hall of Stabbing Westward and The Dreaming, leading up to a full-length album planned for next year. Sorrow Stories and Christopher Hall’s ‘So Sick’ “So Sick” follows “Too Early [with Christopher Hall],” the pair’s first joint release, which came out on April 3, 2026, as an EP featuring remixes from Bow Ever Down, Null Device and Allie Frost. “So Sick” is described as the second track in the ongoing collaboration between Forlorn and Hall, with further material building toward a joint album. About Sorrow Stories Sorrow Stories is the project of UK artist Tina Forlorn, who writes, sings, produces, mixes and masters her own music across dark electro, darkwave, synthpop, EBM, industrial, alt-acoustic and soundtrack styles. Forlorn has self-released her work through Bandcamp since around 2009, after starting out with acoustic demos before moving into electronic production. Her soundtrack work includes music for the horror film “Swap,” released through Epic Pictures, and the short film “Tamesis Trilogy 1” with director Dennis Da Silva, which won the Jean-Luc Godard award for best experimental short in 2020. Sorrow Stories has previously collaborated with Aiboforcen on the 2024 album “Between Noise and Silence” and related EPs, with Aesthetische on the 2021 EP “Overflow,” and with Psy’Aviah on the “Bittersweet” album and its “Healing” and “Still Healing” EPs. Forlorn is currently working with Christopher Hall of Stabbing Westward and The Dreaming on new joint material, of which “So Sick” is the second release following April 2026’s “Too Early” EP.

文 飯田有抄 クラシック音楽ファシリテーター 1974年生まれ。東京藝術大学音楽学部楽理科卒業、同大学院修士課程修了。Maqcuqrie University（シドニー）通訳翻訳修士課程修了。2008年よりクラシ... 詳しく見る 誰もが楽しめる音楽祭 ［サラダ音楽祭 TOKYO MET SaLaD MUSIC FESTIVAL］は、2018年の開幕以来、東京・池袋の東京芸術劇場を中心に開催されている音楽祭だ。「サラダ」の由来は「Sing and Listen and Dance」の頭文字。その名のとおり「歌う、聴く、踊る」というコンセプトに重ねられた、フレッシュで彩り豊かなプログラム編成で、世代を問わず誰もが楽しめるフェスティヴァルである。 2026年の最大のニュースは、メインプログラムがこれまでの2日間から3日間へと拡大されることだ。初日9月11日の夜は、毎年フェスティヴァルの締めくくりを飾ってきた音楽祭メインコンサートが、祭典の幕開けへと据え直される。 東京都交響楽団を指揮するのは梅田俊明。仙台フィルハーモニー管弦楽団の常任指揮者を6年にわたって務め、国内の主要オーケストラへの客演を通じて、堅実かつしなやかな音楽づくりを聴かせてきた。メインコンサートの初登壇となる今回、その円熟した手腕がどのような響きを引きだすか、楽しみだ。新国立劇場合唱団の緻密で広がりある合唱と、金森穣率いるNoism Company Niigataの圧倒的で洗練された身体表現、そして都響とが立体的に織りなす公演となるだろう。 続く12日と13日には、0歳から入場できる「OK！オーケストラ」が両日開催へと拡張され、親子で楽しめるダンス公演「動物たちのダンス＆ミュージック」も新企画として登場。 さらに昨年好評を博した子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』も再演され、家族で味わえる本格的な舞台体験が広がる。SaLaDワークショップやアンサンブルレッスン、ヤマハと共同開発した「だれでもピアノ®」など、聴くだけにとどまらない参加型コンテンツの厚みも、この音楽祭ならではの特徴だ。 多摩・島しょ地域へと届けられる「OK！ オーケストラ in 多摩」や「SaLaDプレミアムコンサート」も今年さらに充実し、街と街、人と人、世代と世代をやわらかにつなぐ。秋の東京に、音楽の喜びが響き合う3日間がやってくる！ 音楽祭メインコンサート《Boléro》～ 音楽と舞踏の豪奢プログラム 好評の《ボレロ》は今年も目玉の一つ。華やかに名曲たちが奏でられる ©サラダ音楽祭実行委員会 「音楽祭メインコンサート《Boléro》」は祭典の幕開けを飾るにふさわしい、豪奢にして緻密なプログラム。指揮を執るのは梅田俊明である。NHK交響楽団や読売日本交響楽団など国内主要オーケストラと共演を重ねるヴェテランの登壇は、本音楽祭にとっても新たな色合いをもたらすに違いない。 昨年SaLaDプレミアムコンサートを指揮した梅田俊明が今年はメインを振る ©K.Miura 前半はグリーグ「組曲《ホルベアの時代より》」で北欧的な清冽さを響かせ、続くラター《グローリア》では、新国立劇場合唱団の輝かしい歌声が天井高くこだまするだろう。後半はラヴェル「組曲《マ・メール・ロワ》」が鮮やかなオーケストレーションで物語を紡ぎ、Noism Company Niigataとのコラボレーションが始まる。 そして、いよいよラヴェル《ボレロ》へ。サラダ音楽祭の象徴的演目ともなりつつあるこの演目は、Noism Company Niigataの舞踏が、凛々しく力強い身体表現で東京都交響楽団とのコラボレーションを展開する。希望や光を感じさせる音楽と舞踏の圧倒的世界に、聴衆は再び息を呑むことになるだろう。 OK！ オーケストラ～0歳から入場OK！ 家族みんなで楽しむ1時間 0歳から入場可能な「OK！ オーケストラ」は、毎年大好評を博してきた人気プログラムだ。今年は土・日の2日間開催へと拡大される。タクトを振るうのは川瀬賢太郎。その伸びやかな音楽作りで、子どもから大人まで魅了する指揮者だ。司会には子ども向けTV番組でおなじみの小林顕作、ダンスは近藤良平率いるコンドルズ、児童合唱は東京少年少女合唱隊と、舞台はにぎやかな顔ぶれで埋め尽くされる。 プログラムもじつに贅沢だ。すぎやまこういち「交響組曲《ドラゴンクエストV》」から、ビゼー《カルメン》、ロッシーニ「《セビリャの理髪師》序曲」、シャブリエ《スペイン》まで、子どもも大人も心拍数が上がるような名曲がずらり。指揮体験コーナーや、客席も一体になって歌うコーナーもあり。声を出しても、身体を動かしてもOK！ 家族みんなで音楽の喜びそのものを体感する、かけがえのない1時間となるだろう。 意地悪なトロールの女王に連れ去られたしろくまのヴァレモンを追って、心優しく勇敢な少女ラグナが冒険の旅へと踏み出す──昨年大好評を博した東京芸術劇場制作の子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』が再演される。 items.body:
Peak Oil sublabel FO returns with a strong debut of late night, air-fried trip hop from Cold Light, flocking like moths to an illbient flame tipped FFO Jabu, Tricky, Sleepdial, Shell Company, Space Afrika.

Cold Light are Bristol’s Birthmark & Withdrawn, Portland’s Best Available Technology, Rael & Eldon out of London, and Hungarian CSNL. Some half a decade after a ‘Live at the Laundromat’ tape introduction, the collective unveil ‘Coldtron 2’, a sparingly sensuous slant on the lush pastures between trip hop, smoked-out dub soul and illbient jazz, inflected with the voices of Elaine Malone, Akeko and British-Nigerian sound designer Tony Onuchukwu. With remarkable restraint - especially considering so many hands are on board - they keep everything pared-back to creaking, atmospheric fundamentals for 40 minutes of smouldering storytelling, passing the torch across chapters of zoot-end poetic monologues, from stylised rap to spoken word, in a spectrum of accents speaking to the group’s far flung coordinates. 

Call it downbeat neo-noir or trip hop 2.0, the sound is clearly in thrall to the ‘90s OGs - Tricky, Portishead, Massive Attack - yet gauzily distinguished from its forebears by the production’s pall of dematerialised textures and an enervated feel for screwed subs and glimmers of sounds that emerged in trip hop’s fall-out. The Bristol night air is thick with sferic crackle and diffused sax in ’Smoke Signal’ thru the Memotone-esque eldritch of ‘Troposphere Test’, taking in a tacit nod to Mobb Deep via Tricky on the smouldering ‘Riot’, or even Civilistjävel!’s low-key electrodub in ‘Lean Wid It…’,    and Sleepdial’s slurred drums on ‘I’ve Known Fires’. But they’re most potent on ‘Fields in B’ with eight mins of smudged Rhythm & Sound steppas bass anchoring the bluest sax plumes and blunted bars, ideal for ashtray dreamers.

items.body:
Topdown Dialectic’s solo debut bow on False Aralia rounds up over a decade of material in supremely elusive style & pattern - all rug-pulling rhythms and hallucinatory fractals wrapped up with proper, hyperreal frisson. Massive chef’s kiss FFO Vladislav Delay, Beatrice Dillon, Paperclip Minimiser, Purelink, Marc Leclair.

An artist keenly observed since initial gestures on /\\Aught in the early ‘10s, and throughout their cult LP trilogy for Peak Oil during 2018-2021; Topdown Dialectic has become a unique facet of C.21st dub electronics, adored for their grasp of diffused spatio-textural sorcery and wraithlike grooves. Anyone paying close attention to emergent sounds via Peak Oil and its False Aralia offshoot may have guessed at TD’s signature, watermarked imprint on the Borgesian Term EP of late ’25, which can now be confirmed as the work of one and the same Izaak Schlossmann; a photographer and producer patently in possession of heightened proprioceptions and a rewardingly patient approach to lushly dissociative sonification. In other words, he makes some of the sexiest electronic music out there - stuff that genuinely feels like it was made this century - and his latest practically leaves you kissing the sky thru its 80 minutes of lip-biting, skin tingling pressure. 

On 16 tracks timed at exactly 5 minutes each, we’re placed in the presence of suggestive sorcery, eliding unarchived material and jams in a unique ecology of oneiric physics. Never overtly showy or overblown, there’s nevertheless a staggering level of ingenuity and synaesthetic effect to its detailed construction and gaseous fractals resembling the LSD or DMT experience. The label themselves compare its nuance to “the flicker of a candle over a desk of drum machines in a Midwestern basement, or the “first blush of sunlight over a tiny campground as subwoofers creak in the distance”, which proves a perfectly poetic analog to its digitally-smudged refractions and tongue-tip spectral tumescence. 

Ultimately, it’s a singular pleasure to immerse the senses in Topdown Dialectic’s self-contained soundsphere, and never more substantially so than on ‘False LP A’. Longtime enthusiasts will surely recognise his skill in parsing salient aspects of Basic Channel x Rhythm & Sound, and their descendants in Vladislav Delay or Pole, reframing those templates in far more uncertain space with a real animist magick. Each work feels tangibly, ambiguously alive, breathing with dynamics and more voluminous, macro scales, and iridescent with voices and details that commands attentive listeners who will have a field day zoning in/out to its illusive, holographic projections and syncopated chronics.

items.body:
London-based "ambient jazz" ace Nala Sinephro steps up her game on 'Endlessness', playfully zig-zagging around an electrifying continuous arpeggio over ten cosmically interlinked tracks assembling decades of spiritual jazz echoing down the line. Fully transcendent material - essential listening for fans of Alice Coltrane, Jon Hassell, Sun Ra, Sons of Kemet, Dorothy Ashby, Laraaji.

It's Sinephro's boundless ambition that bubbles to the surface on 'Endlessness'. She was ever so subtly bold on her debut 'Space 1.8', sensing out a connection between ecstatic ambient music and contemporary jazz that unfolded with gentle, measured charm. Here, she lets her imagination run wild, weaving her historical narrative with vivid, lively threads from across the musical spectrum. Jazz, specifically the spiritual strain that Coltrane, Sanders et al cultivated in the '60s, forms the album's musical backbone, and Sinephro jumps off from that point, infusing familiar tempos with lush modular electronics, uncompromising angular rhythms and sparkling orchestral flourishes. Like Sun Ra's most mischievous work, it's music that betrays a voracious appetite for hierarchy-free admiration - Sinephro is clearly a literate listener, and her passion for sounds as they stretch across borders is palpable from the beginning.

So how might you connect such a wide litany if inspirations? Sinephro opts to balance her energy with a single arpeggio that runs throughout the entire album, using its relative stasis to provoke considerations about the album's central theme. If the concept  is a way to show how the composer-performer is able to add new ingredients to an established form, Sinephro follows the concept aesthetically, refreshing her mode constantly while retaining a recognisable sonic through-line. Her inspiration is "life cycles and rebirth", and from track to track, she reconfigures the logic of a single core idea. 'Continuum 1' sets the initial pace with a waterfall of evolving bleeps and delicate harp chimes; fidgety drums and muted horns follow to help cast our mind through jazz history, but Sinephro doesn't let the track stagnate for a moment. In the middle section, glossy cinematic strings - provided by Orchestrate’s 21 players - intertwine with Sinephro's woozy synths and Morgan Simpson's 'On The Corner'-inspired tempo-fluxing rhythms and we're transported into a different realm entirely.

The hyperactivity continues on 'Continuum 2' as Sinephro obscures the root arpeggio in a verdant tangle of piano, horn and precise percussion that's queered by her giddy psychoacoustic processes. And the mood shifts completely when we reach the gorgeous 'Continuum 3'; Sinephro's arpeggio is hushed to a lullaby-like sine wave crawl that's woken up by her lively harp improvisations. Soon, she interrupts the mood with fusion-era synth jabs, bringing the orchestra back to add some cautious schmaltz that's repeatedly challenged - most obviously on 'Continuum 5', a brief interlude that sounds like Wendy Carlos vs. Blue Note. And when we hit the album's first big interlude, 'Continuum 6', it's a payoff that brings Sinephro's parallel universes together, coddling her hard-panned oscillations with brittle, upfront beats and Sam Gendel-like pitch-bent swoons. Study a little closer, and there are fireworks in even the album's most delicate moments: 'Continuum 8' is a clear highlight that distorts the album's logic with R&B smooveness, and 'Continuum 9', a rare (almost) drumless composition, cements Sinephro's commitment to early electronic music, pushing her synths into the foreground as the album waltzes to its conclusion.

On the finale, Sinephro fires every musical synapse, turning her arpeggio into swooping runs that duck and dive across itchy beats and Alice Coltrane-like ecstatic synth solos, and as it comes to a close, the chaos is calmed with a muted piano that's tape-fluttered until it gasps a final breath. Remarkable music.

items.body:
Remastered reissue of This Heat’s hugely innovative and pioneering anti-rock classic, 1979,  this time on their own, eponymous label. A true milestone in the mutation of pop, rock, avant-garde and electronic music, and arguably post-punk's ground-zero, This Heat consolidated a wealth of music before its arrival whilst casting irrevocable influence over a generation of musicians, producers and engineers in its wake.

Formed in mid ‘70s Brixton, South London, around the trio of Charles Hayward, Charles Bullen and Gareth Williams (later of Flaming Tunes fame), the group drew on and experimented within a flux of sonic disciplines - concrète, pop, dub, and krautrock - to align their mutual ligaments and oppositional structures in a complex, dissonant mass of finely edited improvisations.

Spooling tape noise Testcards jar abruptly with bursts of taut, buzzing drums and metallic guitar squall in Horizontal Hold, before Williams appears as a lamenting ghost, wallowing in the funereal folk drone of Not Waving, and like Damo Suzuki’s shy opposite against the motorik flight of Twilight Furniture.

The album’s definitive moment is still to come, however, with the 2-bar lick of Hayward’s propulsive drums spun thru devilish reverbs and delays in the legendary 24 Track Loop marking a pivotal moment in flux between dub, punk and electro-acoustic music, before the record closes out with Fall of Saigon’s melancholy dirge pop, which clearly set a template for everyone from Hot Chip to Animal Collective or Micachu and the Shapes.

Perhaps understandably, This Heat were never intended as a commercial proposition but, thru the support of John Peel they were able to reach and beguile a national radio audience who probably weren’t ready for them. Thus, their boundary-oblivious virus was planted in the fertile minds of ’79, when punk had already eaten itself and new ideas were definitely required.

By using a minimalist, rhythmically-focussed palette, rent by great minds using the studio-as-instrument, This Heat represents a crucial transition or phase-shift in music from stratified styles toward a union of what might have been formerly perceived as mutually exclusive sounds or styles; boldly following a path out of genre restriction and dilating the dimensions of sonic possibility in the process.

A stone cold classic.

items.body:
Catholics Against Architecture release "Columns" via Fourth Dimension.

"Catholics Against Architecture is the name Chris Connelly has given this project that here collects twelve songs crafted from sonic collages, spoken word, fractured melodies, vocals not far removed from those that David Bowie traded some of his best songs on, rivulets of subdued noise and seemingly random location recordings, tender guitar work, tape manipulation and all kinds of other sounds either in between or beyond. Together, these compositions sit outside convention and pay little regard to whatever the so-called zeitgeist may or may not happen to be. If anything, they draw from his own wonderfully rich past, beginning with his co-founding of avant-garde post-punk outfit Finitribe and moving on through his involvement with Revolting Cocks and various other Al Jourgensen-helmed groups before joining Martin Atkins’ ambitious Pigface project and then more or less operating as an artist under his own name. In the decades since he began his artistic career in the early ’80s, he has maintained this experimental disposition while embracing everything from art-pop and rock to the industrial noise he first cut his teeth on. To place him in a comfortable box would do nothing but serve his defiant temperament some kind of injustice.

“Columns” is no exception. It’s an album that incorporates many ideas and keeps moving while still somehow magically adding up to a whole that gels and seems to make perfect sense. From its occasionally lo-fi stature (due to being recorded on antiquated reel to reel and various cassette players in a state of disrepair) to its jittery blend of free jazz, tone poetry, labyrinthine textural currents and found sounds, passages of hiss and mature songcraft, it points to an artist perfectly at ease with his position as somebody capable of juggling many ideas. Thematically bound to an anti-religion stance which makes sense in these especially turbulent times where rampant polarisation is galvanised by religion as well as politics, “Columns” stands as a testament to something that can never be compounded enough. The title itself, replete with ironic quotation marks, subtly refers to the columns found within churches as well as the columns of smoke generated by religious war.

Ultimately, the album witnesses an artist continuing to explore new trajectories, further prod at ideas that perhaps already presented themselves, and remain true to his place as someone far more than the sum of his parts."

items.body:
The first release on Jim O'Rourke's legendary Moikai imprint in over two decades, 'Spectral Evolution' is a defining statement from Portuguese vanguard Rafael Toral, an album of subtly orchestral, jazz-inspired guitar music that's been slowed to a vertiginous crawl. Using his arsenal of hand-made synths to sing like birds around stretched, steel-wound drones, he evokes Bach, Loren Connors, Gavin Bryars and Rhys Chatham on a longform piece full of conventional chord progressions and alchemical sleights of hand that will have you reeling, and no mistake.

Toral's been through a number of discrete phases since he emerged in the early '90s with 'Sound Mind Sound Body' and 'Wave Field', injecting rock's vigour and emotionality into often cold, academic electronic music. Since then he's described his musical outlook as "post-free jazz", and spent time developing his ‘Space Program’, an ensemble of self-built electronic instruments that helped him evolve his understanding of place and silence. Toral drew a line under that project in 2017 after 13 years of experimentation, and has been working to reconcile his past and present, bringing back the guitar and re-examining the glacial, elongated tonal work he investigated early in his career. 'Spectral Evolution' is his most complete and advanced recording in years, billed as his "quintessential album of guitar music" but inhabiting a unique spot in his catalog. 

Unashamedly romantic, Spectral Evolution pulls its momentous chordal shifts from jazz, using standards like George Gershwin's 'I Got Rhythm' and Duke Ellington's 'Take the "A" Train' (plus what sounds to us quite a lot like Bach) to dictate the course of his vacillating compositions. If that's hard to imagine, it only gets more knotty from there, as Toral interrupts the calm of his tidal drones with chirping oscillator squeaks and squeals that he's painstakingly tuned to harmonise with the strings. Bruising the sublime, Toral reminds us that music is an endless conversation with the past, both our own personal history, and a shared cultural memory that's not always easy to decipher.

After a brief, naked intro, Toral sinks into 'Changes', an outstretched composition that sounds like multiple threads being tied together in real-time. At the root is a sequence of dramatic chord shifts made from bowed guitar drones that have been shaped to sound like orchestral flourishes. We can't help but think of Gavin Bryars' enduringly influential 'Sinking of the Titanic' here, but the chorus of whoops and wails from Toral's arsenal shuttle it into an idiosyncratic outerzone, sounding electronic and acoustic at once, like bamboo flutes, amphibian mating calls and robotic birds responding to each chord. Each track dissolves into the next, and while Toral makes distinctive gestures, the album plays like a continuous thought. 

He interprets 'Take the "A" Train' more literally on 'Take the Train', letting the guitar chords linger and using the Space ensemble to re-imagine the trad standard's unmistakable lead. Peculiarly tuned, it's not obvious at first, but squint a little and you can just about make out Toral coaxing us into re-evaluating how we listen to jazz. If innovators like Ornette Coleman and Albert Ayler were able to develop a new language using familiar syntax, then Toral follows a traditional vernacular, nodding to folk forms as well as avant developments and environmental musics in a mode that’s both soothing and unexpected.

On ‘First Long Space' Toral takes a moment to deconstruct his soundscape, the guitar drawing discernible, post-rock outlines, leaving us with near silence for a few seconds before another episode begins. These spaces (two long and two short) are important markers that break up each episode, palate cleansers that prepare us for further chordal complexity. While 'Fifths Twice' is gooey and sentimental, 'Your Goodbye', is led by distorted, filtered guitar syllables, sounding like Toral's attempt at half-speed blues, played alongside sticky orchestral sweeps. Before the set's over completely, he can't resist taking us to church, mutating his noises into celestial organ blasts on 'Second Short Space'. 

‘Spectral Evolution' is the kind of album that practically urges you to go in again and again to tunnel through its layers and excavate its myriad references and philosophies. It's Toral's most exceptional, essential album to date - the kind of masterpiece worthy of re-booting Moikai to life, the same label that brought us all-timers like Nuno Canavarro's 'Plux Quba', Pita's 'Get Out' and Fennesz's 'Plays'. 

An early marker for AOTY, no doubt.

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interluuds, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.

items.body:
Trading rave for augmented rock, Charli XCX follows the epochal 'brat' with an album that gets ahead of the curve, exciting its indie sleaze and Copenhagen-wave pop backdrop with casual memories from her last two years on the cultural front line.

Before you even try to talk about the music itself, you've gotta get past the cover: a black-and-white photograph of Martin Scorsese, John Cale and Marc Jacobs. There were easier references Aitchison could have made, auteurs who her sizeable audience could have connected to without having to scrape Wikipedia, but it's a statement. When 'brat' blew up - probably beyond even her team's expectations - Aitcherson suddenly found herself on an A-list she'd only grazed in the past. She'd had critical success before, but this was universal acclaim paired with commercial power - she even had the summer of 2024 named after the album. And since then she's been cautiously ubiquitous, acting in a handful of odd indie films, penning the soundtrack to Emerald Fennell's blockbuster 'Wuthering Heights' and producing 'The Moment', a film loosely based on her 'brat' touring experiences. She understands that her place in the pop canon is basically defined by her good taste; if Taylor Swift represents capital itself - the (white) product of the American system, the daughter of a stockbroker and a marketing exec - Aitchison represents the very edge of the mainstream. It's no surprise that she's allying with notorious rebels like Cale, when you think about it.

Of course, 'Music, Fashion, Film' isn't anywhere near as daring as 'The Marble Index' or 'Desertshore', but it is daring all the same. Aitchison follows the club hedonism of 'brat', an album that reasonably could have been released at any time in the last decade, with one that pre-empts a sea change before it's really taken hold. If you've been looking carefully, you'll have noticed that the iron grip electronic music has had on pop has started to loosen; for the first time in decades rock seems to be attractive to young audiences again. Of course, the writing's been on the wall. And then there's the knotty business of AI - it's far more complicated to clone a sloppy indie band than it is to replicate pristine club sounds. Aitchison doesn't throw the baby out with the bath water here - the album is still propped up by A.G. Cook's brushed aluminium productions - but as she says on opener 'Rock Music': "I think the dancefloor is dead / So now we're making rock music."

The aesthetic touch stone here is Daft Punk, though. Aitchison's voice, contorted as she recounts her recent experiences, sounds like it's a bright analogue synth away from 'Human After All'. But the stuttering guitars - already a meme thanks to 'Rock Music' - are refreshingly modish. 'Card Declined' is delivered with the cocaine-assisted sneer of Manhattan's "indie sleaze" scene, while early highlight 'Camera' is genuinely vulnerable ("it makes me want to throw my life away," she says about being on film), with soaring riffs that plant New Order in Paris. With its gloomy cellos and distorted wails, 'I'm Afraid' is probably the album's most uncompromising track (certainly its least "pop"), but the stand-out for us is the finale, when David Cronenberg cuts in with a monologue over woozy organs. "They are dead, they are gone / no-one lasts for ever," he repeats until the album grinds to a halt.

items.body:
Produced by Neek and Jabu's Amos Childs (aka O$VMV$M), Manonmars' third album is syrupy suite of smoke-hazed recollections and free associated reflections set to decelerated bumps, sluggish samples and cloudy drones = sturdy biz FFO Young Echo, Massive Attack, Cold Light, Ka, MIKE, King Vision Ultra, Coby Sey.

Manonmars' 2018 debut is one of those albums we still go back to periodically. It's that rare meeting of minds: a space for O$VMV$M to flex their production muscle and a scratchpad for London-based MC, painter and photographer Jack Martyn Richardson to sketch out a distinct vision of England. And His experiences and impressions on 'Entertainment System' still feel chewable. "Goddess on my arm and both our phones got no service," he quips on 'Goddess'. "Acid is lysergic, psychedelic rock is Turkish." His rhymes aren't throwaway, they map out an underground that's very recognisable, shadowed by O$VMV$M's tuff, effective soundscapes - beats that reference trip-hop, ambient music, exotica and '70s movie soundtracks as much as they do US rap. 

On opener 'Flam3throw3r', Mars raps in double-time over shrill horns that blot out any trace of a beat; Neek and Childs sound as if they relish the negative space, adding chic sword swipes to a track that's got little else to do with the Wu Tang Clan. When a lumbering beat kicks in on 'Decathlon', flipping from downtempo to no-tempo in the final act, it sounds as if it's just there to assert O$VMV$M's commitment to slowness - Mars doesn't even seem to notice, rhyming casually but never losing his flow.

Bristol mainstays Franco Franco and Dali de Saint Paul turn up to assist on 'Volcanic Shield', one of the album's most conventional bangers, led by O$VMV$M's skittering Surf Gang-like beats and morse code blips, and cold light's Birthmark lends his voice to 'Infinite', going bar for bar with Mars over Neek and Childs' slackened funk, blaring out like an old tape on a busted in-car audio system. 'Firewater' takes the same approach, leaving Mars to do his best as snares splash across the spectrum with added sax from Brum-based sound artist Lorenzo Prati. "My bitch white, she can scuba dive and ice climb," he spits. "Put the drink down, I wasn't in my right mind." 

It's music that laughs through the tears - what could be more British than that?

items.body:
One of the most influential, insular and multi-layered albums of the last five decades, created through endless hours of improvisation - involving almost fifty musicians and recorded in complete darkness, 'Spirit Of Eden' was a radical departure for Talk Talk, ' an album that has attained almost mythical status since its release in 1988.

Following the commercial success of their singles "It's My Life", "Life's What You Make It” and album "The Colour of Spring”, Talk Talk retreated into the shadows and produced an album that still defies categorisation. Mark Hollis is said to have demanded the players record in almost complete darkness, improvising for hours to produce individual parts without hearing any backing tracks or surrounding material.

"Spirit Of Eden" is one of the most fearless and rewarding leaps a commercially successful band has ever taken, and continues to cast its influence almost 40 years later.

items.body:
Somewhere between more eaze, Susan Alcorn and Daniel Lanois, 'Langliek', the first album from pedal-steel masters Geir Sundstøl and Joe Harvey-Whyte, is a taste of bliss, a hazy, horizontal duet on guitar, organ, Moog and drum machine.

It's hard not to immediately warm to this one. The pedal-steel's an underused instrument, to be honest, and one that suits "ambient" music remarkably well, we've known this at least since Lanois introduced it to Brian Eno's arsenal of sounds on the milestone 'Apollo: Atmospheres and Soundtracks'. And even though Norwegian multi-instrumentalist Sundstøl and London-based player Harvey-Whyte have been refining their craft individually for years, the latter playing with everyone from Josephine Foster to Billy Bragg and the former contributing to literally hundreds of albums, it's that record that still serves as the creative anchor for their collaboration.

The duo began chatting in 2016 when Harvey-Whyte discovered Sundstøl's solo album 'Furulund', and they continued chatting and visiting each others' studios until 2024 when Harvey-Whyte took a break from touring to spend a week in Oslo. They worked spontaneously, which was a surprise for Sundstøl, who usually spends months tweaking each little detail, and relied on their improvisations on pedal-steel to set the pace of each piece. Adding elements from Sundstøl's arsenal of instruments (including an Optigan, a rare optical keyboard, and a set of Moog synths, the duo turned their improvisations into a full album, conjuring up a mood that genuinely felt Norwegian.

Of course, it's hard to separate the instrument from its American roots, but the duo pull out the edges of Americana just far enough to justify the album's title, a reference to a Norwegian folk instrument. You can just about hear the snow crunching in the background and see a hint of neon green in the sky, if you look carefully.

items.body:
All upward lift and kosmiche synth iridescence from Seoul’s blissed family band, back on the Far East’s leading krautrock revival label, Guruguru Brain...

“The blissed family band is back! TENGGER have always moved together, through time, space & genre. 'SKY' arrives as a new chapter: a little more still, a little more inward, while keeping all the warmth that's always been at the heart of what they do.

Embodying the band name meaning "endless sky" in Mongolian and "vast sea" in Hungarian, their 8th album 'SKY' centres on the feelings of boundless, infinite expansion. Conceived as one continuous environment rather than a collection of tracks, the album unfolds slowly through luminous synths, patient drones and Itta's breath-like vocals.

Like a soft big sky you can actually float on: 'SKY' is vast, warm, and wide open.

"Rather than a specific emotion, we hope the record opens a certain awareness — that the sky is not just something to be seen. Through it, we sense a connection to something much larger — a feeling of being linked to the wider universe. This sense of connection runs through the entire record.””

items.body: After the void on a distant sun (2023) and [limen memoriae] (with Luca Ferro, 2024), Angelo Panebianco and Matteo Mariano return as phoanøgramma with dream flow, a single long-form composition presented in six movements. Although divided into individual tracks for navigation, the work was conceived as an uninterrupted whole, with the titles reading like successive lines of a single poem. From beginning to end, the music remains in constant motion, continually altering density, and texture without ever interrupting its flow. Panebianco establishes the broad harmonic terrain with slowly expanding drones, while Mariano introduces subtle perturbations that keep the surface in perpetual motion. “raindrops (prelude)” begins with rhythmic droplets that gradually dissolve into bubbling textures as broad circular harmonies gather around them before acquiring an insistent metallic edge. “arise in sinking feelings” darkens the atmosphere, introducing currents of unease that quietly unsettle the calm established at the outset. “fractures” opens onto an immense glacial space where deep resonances stretch into the distance while minute electronic activity continues beneath them, gradually generating a dense web of interacting signals. The balance shifts during the second half. “where things are hollow” allows machine-like chatter and electronic circuitry to emerge with increasing clarity before they slowly sink back into the surrounding drone during “a cecasting of indices”. By the closing chapter, “the vanishing”, the droplets heard at the beginning quietly reappear, completing the album’s circular trajectory. Repetition, rotation and inversion shape the work throughout, with recurring materials returning in altered forms as though recalled from memory rather than simply repeated. The six chapters reveal a compositional practice built on serial procedures, recurring materials and gradual transformation. Sounds return altered by context, textures migrate from foreground to background, and seemingly incidental details quietly reshape the listener’s perception of what came before. The result is an album whose continuity arises from the way each recurrence subtly modifies the whole. To guide us through the different undercurrents of the album, Angelo Panebianco and Matteo Mariano have agreed to answer four questions by email. phoanøgramma’s previous releases, from the void on a distant sun to [limen memoriae] — with Luca Ferro — often seemed concerned with memory, distance, thresholds and liminal states. dream flow feels like a continuation of those interests, but also a more fluid and immersive work, unfolding almost as a single dream process rather than a collection of discrete compositions. How do you see this album in relation to your earlier collaborations, and what new territory were you trying to explore together here? You have certainly identified one of the central intentions behind the album: the idea of fluidity and immersion. In this sense, we see this last album as an evolution in terms of intention. Our previous works were also connected to ideas of memory, distance, thresholds and unstable spaces, but they were based on more abstract or suggested concepts. With dream flow, the concept was not only a background suggestion, but a real compositional direction: we wanted to evoke a specific condition, a circumscribed but open-ended image — the continuous transformation of perception inside a dream, in which everything moves continuously, changes shape, dissolves and reappears without clear boundaries. Musically, we also wanted to move toward a more classically ambient/drone form. the void on a distant sun had darker moments, with a strong presence of tapes and synthesizers, while [limen memoriae] had a dimension closer to improvisation and electroacoustic interaction. For dream flow, we worked in a more programmatic way, starting from the concept itself and shaping the material accordingly. It is probably a more carefully studied work, less instinctive in its construction, even though we wanted to preserve the sense of instability and suspension that belongs to the dream state. The title dream flow and the accompanying text suggest a work built around transformation, dissolution and the unstable logic of dreams: “fractures bloom where things are hollow” and “a recasting of indices spirals toward the vanishing.” Were these tracks shaped by specific dreams, subconscious imagery and personal experiences, or are you more interested in creating the conditions under which listeners can project their own dream narratives onto the music? There is certainly a personal inspiration behind dream flow, coming from our own memories of dreams and dreamlike states. One example is the cover image itself, which represents an imaginary environment where sky and earth seem to exchange places. That image was suggested by a childhood dream remembered by Matteo: he was swimming in a lake, looking up at the sky, and beyond the clouds he could see mountains, almost as if he were looking down from above. Of course, it is impossible to translate such an image directly into music. What we tried to do instead was to start from our own personal images and memories, but without turning them into a closed narrative. We wanted to create a sound environment in which the listener could enter freely, bringing their own dream memories and associations into the experience. So the album is not meant to describe a specific dream in a literal way. It is more about creating the emotional and perceptual conditions for a dreamlike process to take place — something that can carry the listener from the beginning to the end, while leaving enough space for their own inner images to emerge. Both of you come from slightly different backgrounds and working methods. Matteo’s recent work on albums such as Magnetic Series explored the materiality and constraints of tape manipulation, while Angelo’s solo work as Phoan often embraces intuition, spontaneity and the search for hidden sounds within sounds. How did those approaches intersect during the making of dream flow? Was the album built through careful composition, improvisation, sound design, or some combination of all three? Having two different ways of working, and two different ways of approaching sound, was actually one of the strengths of the project. At times our methods can seem quite distant from one another, but this distance allows each of us to contribute where we feel more naturally effective. In the case of dream flow, Angelo brought the initial structure of the work and much of the raw drone material that runs through the whole album. Matteo’s role was more connected to a later stage of manipulation and construction: taking the material generated by Angelo and working on it in a more architectural way, assembling, reshaping and refining the overall form. So the album was born from a combination of intuition, sound design and careful composition. The intuitive element was essential in generating the first material and discovering the hidden qualities within it, but the final shape of the album came through a more deliberate process of editing, transformation and structural control. We were interested in preserving the organic nature of the original sounds, while giving them a clear long-form direction. The album is presented as six separate tracks with a continuous mix. Listening to it feels less like moving from one composition to another than drifting through different states within the same dream. Indeed the track titles read like verses from a single poem. How did you approach shaping that long-form narrative? Were you thinking in terms of tension and release, recurring motifs, or even something closer to cinematic editing, where one scene dissolves into the next without a clear boundary? We approached the album as a single long-form piece divided into six moments, rather than as six fully separate compositions. The track division gives the listener a possible map, but the real form of the album is the continuous flow. In shaping that flow, we were probably closer to the idea of cinematic editing than to a traditional sequence of individual pieces. We were interested in transitions, dissolves, changes of density and perspective — the way one sound environment can slowly become another without a clear boundary. In a dream, scenes often change in this way: you do not always perceive the exact moment of transformation, but suddenly you find yourself somewhere else. There are forms of tension and release, but not in a dramatic or narrative sense. They are more connected to perception: expansion and contraction, presence and distance, saturation and emptiness, moments of greater density followed by more suspended or rarefied passages. Some materials and gestures return, but often in altered forms, as if they were memories of something already heard rather than clearly recognizable motifs. The choice of titles also follows this idea of a fluid dream state. Each title can be read individually, as if it framed a specific moment or image within the dream, but the titles can also be read in sequence, almost as a single poetic line that describes the entire oneiric process. In that sense, they are not simply names for separate tracks, but fragments of the same movement. For this reason, we considered it very important to present the album as a continuous mix. This was also taken into account for the physical CD edition: the album is conceived as a single uninterrupted flow, divided into individual tracks that function more as indices of a whole than as autonomous pieces. (Gianmarco Del Re)
